study_identification.author_journal_year: Kim et al., Biological Psychiatry Global Open Science, 2025
study_identification.title: Predicting Mental and Neurological Illnesses Based on Cerebellar Normative Features

study_characteristics.study_objective: To test the value of individual deviations from normative cerebellar development across the lifespan for prediction of autism spectrum disorder, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, mild cognitive impairment, and Alzheimer's disease using machine learning, and to identify cerebellar regions that contributed most to the prediction.

dataset_name.answer: Multi-site aggregated dataset (ABIDE I and II; ADNI; AIBL; DEMGEN; TOP; and other studies from the cerebellar lifespan normative model)

hc_n.answer: 27117 (training set); 26985 (test set); matched controls varied by clinical cohort (AD:116, ASD:317, BD:238, MCI:122, SZ:195)

hc_age.answer: Training set: mean 54.36, SD 20.31; Test set: mean 54.52, SD 19.19; Age range 3 to 85 years; Matched HC varied by clinical cohort

hc_sex.answer: Training set: F 53%, M 47%; Test set: F 53%, M 47%; Matched HC sex distribution varied by clinical cohort

preprocessing_pipeline.answer: FreeSurfer v5.3 (skull stripping); FSL v6.0 (fslreorient2std, FLIRT linear registration); ENIGMA Cerebellum Volumetric Pipeline with ACAPULCO algorithm (cerebellar parcellation); N4 correction (inhomogeneity correction); ANTs (registration to ICBM 2009c template in MNI space); SUIT v3.4 (cerebellar gray and white matter voxel-based morphometry)

quality_checking_detail.answer: Automated quality control using ENIGMA Cerebellum Volumetric Pipeline QC Scripts of ACAPULCO with Singularity. Participants with extreme outliers (2.698 SD above or below the mean) in more than 2 lobules were excluded based on automated quality control measures. Approximately 5% of scans were manually inspected to ensure quality and consistency. Quality control pipeline included quantitative and visual information on volumetric aspects including volume, outliers, and box plots. Participants were excluded if scans revealed outliers in at least two regions, or when a scanning site contributed data from fewer than five participants.

site_effect_handling_detail.answer: Bayesian linear regression with likelihood warping method (incorporating sinarcsinh transformation) to handle nonlinear basis functions and non-Gaussian predictive distributions for large datasets. Scanning site was accounted for as a fixed effect. The normative model accounts for sex, age, and scanning site.

model_origin_detail.answer: Publicly available cerebellar normative model based on approximately 27,000 individuals without diagnoses, developed by Kim et al. (2024) published in Nature Mental Health. The cerebellar normative model spans ages 3 to 85 years and includes cerebellar lobules and voxelwise intensities, adjusting for sex, age, and scanning site. See Kim et al., Nature Mental Health 2:1196-1207, 2024.

modeling_method.answer: Bayesian linear regression with likelihood warping (wBLR)

software_tool.answer: Not explicitly stated for normative modeling implementation (likely PCNtoolkit based on methods); scikit-learn v1.2.2 (for logistic regression and random forest); XGBoost v1.7.3

response_variable.answer: Cerebellar lobular volumes (28 lobules); Voxelwise gray matter intensities mapped onto cerebellar atlases

predictor_effects.answer: Scanning site: fixed effect; Age and Sex: modeled in the normative framework (specific fixed/random designation not detailed for these variables)

nm_vldtn_handle_ns.reason: The study explicitly handles nuisance structure through multiple mechanisms: (1) Bayesian linear regression with likelihood warping method incorporates sinarcsinh transformation to handle non-Gaussian predictive distributions, (2) scanning site is modeled as a fixed effect to account for site differences, (3) age and sex are explicitly adjusted for in the normative model, and (4) quality control procedures exclude extreme outliers. The likelihood warping method specifically addresses non-normality in the data distribution.
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.supporting_text: To analyze the data, we utilized Bayesian linear regression with the likelihood warping method (44), incorporating the sinarcsinsh transformation (45,46), to handle nonlinear basis functions and non-Gaussian predictive distributions for large datasets (45). Scanning site was accounted for as a fixed effect (47,48). ... normative model includes cerebellar lobules and voxelwise intensities, which differ across tissues (e.g., gray matter, white matter, cerebrospinal fluid) based on their proton density and relaxation properties, while adjusting for sex, age, and scanning site
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.location: Main text page discussing Normative Modeling section

nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.reason: The normative model provides evaluation metrics calculated in the test set (n=26,985), which is a held-out portion of the same reference cohort used for training. This test set is from the same domain (neurotypical individuals from the same multi-site aggregated dataset) and represents non-independent validation as it comes from the same overall data collection effort.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.supporting_text: individuals without a diagnosis were split into a training set (n = 27,117; 54% female), a test set (n = 26,985; 53% females), and a clinical set (n = 1757; 30% females). ... The normative model provides point estimates and evaluation metrics such as explained variance, mean squared log loss, skew, and kurtosis (46). These evaluation metrics were calculated in the test set, which did not include clinical cohorts.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.location: Methods section, Sample and Normative Modeling subsections

nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.reason: While the test set (n=26,985) is technically held-out from training, it is unclear whether this represents truly independent data collection or simply a random split of the same aggregated dataset. The paper does not explicitly describe whether the test set comes from different scanning sites, different time periods, or represents a prospective validation cohort. The matched controls for clinical cohorts may represent some degree of independent same-domain validation, but this is not clearly articulated as a formal validation strategy.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.supporting_text: individuals without a diagnosis were split into a training set (n = 27,117; 54% female), a test set (n = 26,985; 53% females), and a clinical set (n = 1757; 30% females). ... Individuals without diagnoses were matched to the clinical datasets of patients with AD, ASD, BD, MCI, and SZ (Table 1) using nearest-neighbor matching based on exact matches of sex and scanning site with age as implemented in MatchIt.

nm_vldtn_diff_domain.reason: The normative model trained on healthy controls is applied to predict clinical outcomes in different domain datasets (clinical cohorts with ASD, BD, SZ, MCI, and AD from ABIDE I and II, ADNI, AIBL, DEMGEN, and TOP). This represents cross-domain validation where the model trained on neurotypical individuals is tested on clinical populations with different neurobiological characteristics. The study reports prediction performance (AUROC values) for these different clinical domains.
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.supporting_text: The clinical datasets were obtained from the ABIDE I and II (Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange I and II), ADNI (Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative), AIBL (The Australian Imaging, Biomarkers and Lifestyle Flagship Study), DEMGEN (Norwegian Dementia Genetics Network), and TOP (Thematically Organized Psychosis) cohorts. ... Permutation testing revealed significant predictions for ASD and SZ (AUROC values ranging from 0.56 to 0.65), using various models based on deviations from the cerebellar normative model.
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.location: Methods section Sample subsection and Results section

clinical_dataset.answer: ABIDE I and II (for ASD); ADNI (for AD and MCI); AIBL (for AD); DEMGEN (for AD and MCI); TOP (for BD and SZ)

diseases_studied.answer: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD); Bipolar Disorder (BD); Schizophrenia (SZ); Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI); Alzheimer's Disease (AD)

clinical_groups_age.answer: ASD: mean 12.35, SD 4.42; BD: mean 31.61, SD 11.40; SZ: mean 28.29, SD 9.45; MCI: mean 67.25, SD 9.27; AD: mean 73.11, SD 7.60

deviation_metric.answer: Z-score derived from normative models; Extreme deviations defined as |z| > 1.96 (most extreme 5% in both directions); For each ROI, three statistics were computed: median z-score, variance of z-scores, and percentage of extreme deviations (proportion of voxelwise deviations exceeding |z| > 1.96 threshold)

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: Machine learning classification using logistic regression (LR), random forest (RF), and XGBoost with stratified 5-fold cross-validation; Area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) as primary performance metric; Additional metrics: precision, recall, sensitivity, specificity, balanced accuracy, and area under precision-recall curve; Permutation testing (1000 iterations) to assess statistical significance of AUROC values; Feature importance ranking based on LR coefficients to identify cerebellar regions contributing to predictions; Between-model comparisons using permutation-based approach
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: Cerebellar normative features showed moderate predictive power for ASD and SZ (AUROC 0.56-0.65) but not for BD, MCI, or AD, with contributions from both anterior and posterior cerebellar regions.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: Permutation testing revealed statistically significant predictions for ASD and SZ with AUROC values ranging from 0.56 to 0.65 using various models based on deviations from cerebellar normative models. For SZ, the most predictive models were centered around median and variance measures within ROIs for voxelwise models. For ASD, models based on lobular volumes and voxelwise variance within ROIs were most predictive. Prediction performance for MCI, AD, and BD were not above chance levels. Feature importance analysis for SZ highlighted vermis IX, left IV, regions associated with verbal fluency and autobiographical recall (task-based atlas), left S1 (social-linguistic-spatial) and D1 (demand) regions (hierarchical atlas), and limbic A and somatomotor A networks (resting-state atlas). For ASD, left VIIB and left crus II (anatomical atlas), right VI and left crus II (lobular volumes), and regions linked to narrative/emotion/language processing and right-hand movement (task-based atlas) showed highest feature importance. Random forest and XGBoost approaches showed no notable differences from logistic regression in terms of feature importance or performance, indicating robustness across different modeling approaches.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: Limited predictive power of trained models (AUROC 0.56-0.65) should be interpreted cautiously for clinical application. Harmonizing behavioral, cognitive, genetic, phenotypic, lifestyle, symptomatology, and medical history data across datasets is challenging. Multivariate feature importance must be assessed in overall model context; collinearity among features can cause fluctuations in rankings. Complex clinical conditions are heterogeneous with wide array of symptoms and genetic variations; some individuals may exhibit resilience due to genetic/lifestyle factors complicating predictions. Individual-level interpretation of deviations remains challenging (whether deviations are biologically significant or imaging artifacts). Existence of subgroups within heterogeneous conditions complicates performance metrics. Neurodevelopmental changes raise concerns about appropriateness of applying adult template space and atlases to younger children and adolescents. Only approximately 5% of scans were manually inspected for quality control. Occasional outliers might have been missed despite extensive QC procedures. Cerebellum's distinct position and intricate folding pattern present challenges in obtaining precise MRI data. Future studies should include other brain regions and multimodal approaches. AUROC 0.7-0.8 is acceptable for some clinical applications but may not suffice for many scenarios where 0.8-0.9 is regarded as appropriate.
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: The study demonstrates cerebellar normative modeling can provide moderate discrimination for ASD and SZ but suggests limited immediate clinical utility. Four different cerebellar atlases (anatomical 28 ROIs, task-based 10 ROIs, hierarchical 32 ROIs, resting-state 17 ROIs) enhanced interpretability of findings, though no single atlas consistently emerged as superior. Both motor and cognitive cerebellar regions contributed to SZ prediction, underscoring the disorder's complexity. For ASD, variance of z-scores within parcellations indicated greater voxel-level variability across regions, reflecting the substantial heterogeneity of the condition. The relatively preserved cerebellum in AD/MCI may explain lack of predictive power. The cerebellar normative models from this work are publicly available via PCNportal at https://pcnportal.dccn.nl/.

general_notes.general_notes: This study is a follow-up to Kim et al. (2024) published in Nature Mental Health, which developed the cerebellar normative model used here. The current study focuses specifically on predictive modeling and classification rather than case-control differences. The full sample included 54,102 participants across 132 scanning sites (Supplementary Table 2). Clinical cohorts came from well-established datasets: ABIDE I and II for ASD (n=900 in full clinical set before matching), ADNI for AD (n=146 before matching) and MCI, AIBL for AD, DEMGEN for dementia cohorts, and TOP for BD (n=277 before matching) and SZ (n=312 before matching). The study applied multiple cerebellar atlases to enhance functional interpretation: 28-region anatomical (ACAPULCO segmentation), 10-region multi-domain task battery (King et al. 2019), 32-region hierarchical atlas (Nettekoven et al. 2024), and 17-network resting-state connectivity atlas (Buckner et al. 2011). The normative modeling approach extends pediatric growth chart concepts to brain imaging, preserving individual-level inference. Feature engineering included calculating median, variance, and percentage of extreme deviations for each atlas ROI. The paper was previously published as a preprint on medRxiv. Code availability: FreeSurfer, FSL, ACAPULCO, SUIT, and PCNtoolkit are all open-source and publicly available. The study received funding from multiple Norwegian and European sources including South-Eastern Norway Regional Health Authority, Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft, NordForsk, Research Council of Norway, and European Research Council.
